title: Roman’s guidance tests and first coronagraph images mark a preparation milestone
summary:
A telescope may need to collect light for minutes or hours to reveal faint objects. During that time, even a tiny pointing error can blur an image. NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has completed tests showing that its guidance system can keep the observatory remarkably steady.

Engineers tested the fine-guidance system from September 15 to 21. Roman’s main science instrument, the Wide Field Instrument, has 18 detectors. A small section of each detector rapidly monitors a different guide star: a star whose position is already known with great accuracy.

The spacecraft’s attitude control system first points Roman toward the right region of sky. Fine guidance then tracks the reference stars and reports their positions about four times each second. Those measurements allow the control system to correct small drifts during an exposure.

The tests demonstrated stability better than one hundred-thousandth of a degree for half an hour during Wide Field Instrument observations, or eight hours during Coronagraph Instrument observations. The demonstrated steadiness is roughly comparable to keeping a laser aimed at a U.S. dime from about 240 kilometers away. Engineers expect further tuning to improve it.

Roman will also test a different approach to guidance. Instead of using only a star’s pointlike image, it can use spectra, patterns showing how light is distributed across wavelengths. Roman already measures spectra for science, so the same information could help maintain its position. This guidance mode still needs validation.

The team tested fine guidance together with the Coronagraph Instrument on September 22 and 27. A coronagraph suppresses bright starlight, allowing much dimmer objects around stars to become visible. Roman’s instrument is designed to demonstrate technologies for studying planets and dusty disks around nearby stars. It also has its own internal stability process.

In its first preliminary observation, the coronagraph imaged a faint star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighboring galaxy. The detectors were deliberately warmer than their eventual operating temperature to help prevent contamination from sticking to them. That produced extra image noise.

For the second observation, the team cooled the detectors to improve sensitivity and pointed toward a location expected to contain many stars. Multiple stars appeared, confirming the pointing.

These observations checked that light could pass through the instrument and form a focused image. They begin a careful sequence of increasingly demanding tests.
why_it_matters: The tests check the pointing and imaging abilities Roman needs before attempting more demanding observations of faint objects.
